references.text: Joseph assures his brothers that what they intended for evil, God intended for good to preserve the lives of many people.
The psalmist tells how God called a famine upon the land and sent Joseph ahead of them – he was sold as a slave, but it was part of God's plan.
Stephen recounts that the patriarchs sold Joseph into Egypt out of jealousy, but God was with him and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, who made him ruler over Egypt and his entire household.
Pharaoh puts Joseph in charge of all the land of Egypt, gives him his signet ring, and makes him second most powerful in the kingdom – fulfilling God's plan to send him there.
The king's heart is like water channels in the Lord's hand; he turns it wherever he wishes – an expression of God's sovereignty over human actions.
Direct continuation of the same event: 41:28 introduces God's plan, while 45:8 reveals its fulfilled purpose.
Theological parallel regarding 'sending': Both emphasize that the action or message comes from God, not from the person themselves.
Direct allusion: Stephen retells Joseph's story to highlight God's plan to save His people through him.
